utterances.text: Yes, I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at this second paragraph that my learned friend asked you about in which it says that commander Lubenovic informed you that a platoon, the one from Kotor Varos, no longer wanted to be part of the 306th Mountain Brigade and wanted to join the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's on page 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's on page 1, the beginning of paragraph 2. This fact to which your attention was drawn by Commander Lubenovic, who said that part of his brigade wanted to be transferred to another regular unit, did you consider this to be a significant problem for the commander?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he told me this and added that they were going to other units as well, if you add to this other fighters going to other units, then their number is even greater and of course it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you, sir, read the sentence beginning with "also."

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Also from the Muslim forces"?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Also from the Muslim forces stationed in Mehurici village, a communication was sent to all villages summoning soldiers for a 40-day training. The question rises of a timely rotation of personnel in the Ljuta Greda sector."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the interpreters once again to translate the word in the Bosnian text of this sentence which is that soldiers are being called or invited because the official translation here is that they have received orders. So would you please interpret exactly what the witness said?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You, Mr. Jusufspahic, said that you made notes and that you drew up your report in the command on the basis of your notes. What you wrote down here, was this what Commander Lubenovic told you, that these Muslim forces were receiving letters in the villages where they were calling on people to join them? Is this the problem that you understood to be a serious problem?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is exactly what he said. He used other terms as well, that they were coaxing them, trying to attract them in ways that in my Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond view were not soldierly at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Commander Lubenovic said that they were addressing him or his command, or was the essence of what he said exactly what you wrote down, that they were sending letters to all the villages calling on young men, trying to attract them?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. They were calling on them and trying to attract them through letters, through oral means, trying various ways to get at those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you understood this to be a serious problem about which you had to inform your superior command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the defence line was very drawn out, Ljuta Greda and the other Greda, if you know what it looks like, this is a dominant feature overlooking the villages. And if someone who is in command of that area of defence tells you that there will come a point when they will be unable to organise the defence, of course it's scary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at page 2 where it says "proposed measures," and then look at number 4, proposal number 4 made by you to the superior commands, and you said that you sent this to the lower-level commands for their information, the 306th Mountain Brigade. Tell me please, after this information the corps commander could he make a decision about this situation or inform his superior command if this was not within his competence? Is that how your superior commander operated?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you whether you suggested to the corps commander that he should report about this to his superiors. What I'm asking you now is the following: When you make a proposal to the corps commander, as an officer and a soldier, is it the usual procedure or not for the corps commander to evaluate your proposals and decide what he can make decisions on because it falls within his competence, and whatever is not within his competence he informs his superior commander?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what usually happened, not only in this case but in other cases as well. This was not the only problem we had. This would have been the regular procedure although the corps was still in the process of being formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document numbered 5, which we have only in the Bosnian version, and of which you read out a part of the text. It's number 1404. It's just behind these documents. It's numbered 5. Previously you read the part of the text in which Commander Hadzihasanovic is forwarding to his units an order from the staff of the supreme command --

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would object in light of the fact that this document was not reviewed with the witness during cross-examination, and therefore our submission would be that its improper for the witness to be re-examined on a document that he was shown only during his direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a legal issue. As you know, additional questions have to be connected to the examination-in-chief. This document was not shown during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe it is -- it is linked to the cross-examination in its essence because it mentions soldiers going over to other units, and this order could be the result. I cannot testify for the witness, but in a brief time after this document the staff of the supreme command is regulating the issue of the transfer of these units, the units from Mehurici, which is now -- has become another brigade. I believe that this is connected. But if you will not allow me this question, I will withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead. Put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the document which you read out previously, does it now solve some of the problems you noticed previously, the problem of units wanting to go over to other brigades?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, and this is how the corps operated previously as well, shows that if someone is unable to make a decision they inform their superior commander and the formation of the 27th Motorised Brigade is regulated here and the transfer to other units. This was now under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you are an officer of the army, tell me these proposals of the creation of certain units or declaring certain units to be paramilitary, in whose competence was this?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was within the competence of the highest command. We could not do that at our level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, the highest command was higher than the command of the 3rd Corps. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, higher than the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, you said that you were the commander of the 306th Brigade. Up until which year were you the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was appointed that post in mid-August, but in 1993 when I assumed that post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were wounded in November. After November 1993, where were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the first week of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And afterwards, what sort of responsibilities did you have?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After November 1993 -- well, as you can see, Your Honours, I had a lot of work. I was wounded and I spent a long time in the hospital in Travnik, about a month. I was wounded in the spine. Afterwards, when I recovered, I reported to the corps command. Let me just clarify something. I apologise. There's a document in which it says that I'm being assigned to an operations group, perhaps you have seen it. But I didn't go there, I went to the hospital. I was detained in the hospital, and after I had recovered I was told to report to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you -- when you finished your service in the army, what sort of rank did you have? You left the army with what rank?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the rank of major. But when I was retired, I was promoted to the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the interpretation, you left the army with the rank of colonel. So you were a higher-level officer. We'll have another look at the document presented by the Defence counsel, a document that has already been tendered into evidence by the other Defence team. I deliberately left the document on the ELMO, and you should have a copy before you in your own language. Before I put my question to you, did you know that with regard to what happened in Maline General Merdan, in the month of August 1993, went to the site to observe the three sites, to observe the three sites where people had been buried. Were you aware of this fact? And in addition, he didn't go there on his own; he was accompanied by representatives of the International Community, European Community representatives. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that fact and I never went to that place either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even go to that place with the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You assumed your duties in the month of August, but on which date exactly? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived in the brigade in mid-August. There was a transfer of duties. You know it was a very vast zone, but I assumed my duties towards the end of August. For a certain period of time, there were two commanders who were working in parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Were you aware of the fact that about the 23rd of September to be precise the UN centre of human rights met General Merdan in Zenica. This had to do with what had happened in Maline. Were you aware of this fact or not?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of this. I only received an order at a later date, the order we have been discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of October, two days before the report we have before us, on the 17th of October, Mr. Delic, the highest-ranking military officer sent a letter to the 3rd Corps command informing them of the fact that President Izetbegovic had been contacted by the UN special envoy with regard to the events in Maline. Were you at your level aware of the fact that the question of Maline, the issue of Maline, had been discussed at an international level and that the highest level of state it had been -- it was an issue that had been addressed at the highest level of state by President Izetbegovic. Were you aware of this fact or not.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really wasn't aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You weren't aware of the fact, very well. I had these preliminary questions that I wanted to put to you before discussing the document, because the document states that 25 individuals were killed in the course of combat. This is the document that would be sent up the chain of command and it would make it possible to inform the UN that these people were killed in combat. How is it that the document does not refer to the request made on the 17th of October by the 3rd Corps commander who had asked that the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group draft a report? How is it that there is no reference? How would you explain this? Because when we have a look at the document, the impression one has is that it's a document that was drafted without reference to a request of any kind. It's a document drafted, so to speak, spontaneously. Do you have an explanation of this fact?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked by the Prosecution about Mr. Delalic and the tasks he had to carry out. I don't know why there's no reference here, but to me it is obvious that it refers to that request, or rather that it relates to that request. He should have mentioned this fact. It should be contained in the document, and I don't know why no reference is made to the fact. But it was quite clear to me that there was this relation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When Mr. Asim Delalic drafted this report as commander of the 306th Brigade, there are three copies, so we can see there are three copies for the archives, for the Operational Group, and for the 3rd Corps. My first question is: Before the document was sent, did you read it? Did you yourself read the document before it was forwarded to these addressees? As this happened a long time ago, I know that it might be very difficult to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure that I read the document. Perhaps I was informed about it orally, but I cannot categorically state that I read the document through to the end. But I know that this was the situation. I was familiar with the situation, whether it was on the basis of this document or on the basis of something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had known that on the basis of this document the 3rd Corps commander was going to inform the minister of defence or the chief of staff that there had been men killed in combat, if you had known about this wouldn't you have had to sign the document? If Mr. Izetbegovic was going to be informed of the contents of this document, if that was to be the case wouldn't you have had to sign the document.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a minute ago I said that I didn't realise that that level was in question, too, or rather I didn't realise that Mr. Izetbegovic was familiar with the issue. I wasn't informed of the fact by the corps. I was just asked to report on the events from that period, to report on whether there had been crimes committed. I wasn't aware of the level at which this issue had been addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you had been informed of the fact that the international community was interested in this issue, as commander of the 306th Brigade wouldn't you have launched an investigation to provide you with precise information on the circumstances of which men were killed in combat? Wouldn't you have done more than what was done, as stated in the report? The report states that there were 25 men killed in combat. These men were of Croatian -- had Croatian nationality. Apparently they didn't have any military identity cards on them, but there is nothing else we know about the subject. Would you have launched a more detailed investigation into the matter? Would you have launched a so-called command investigation? That's what we call it in military terms.

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we go back to that period 1993 -- well, you know how it is. It's 2005 now. As far as I can remember at the time, I wasn't aware of the fact that such a request had been made at such a high level. I received an order from the corps command requesting that I provide them with information on the events, events that took place when I wasn't present on the scene. So I really didn't have the faintest idea of the fact that this issue had been discussed at such a high level. That was the situation. According to how I had understood the situation, the men in question were combatants. Perhaps I was mistaken, but that's what I thought. In fact, they were killed in combat; that's how I understood the situation. But as to the fact that the issue had been raised at such a high level, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I have two or three very small questions to put to you on your inspection of the 312th and the 306th Brigades, to start with. You told us that when you inspected the 312th Brigade on the 30th of July you were told that there were some 30 Arabs present there at the front line in the neighbourhood of Bijelo Bucje. And the next day you inspected the 306th Brigade and you were confronted with the presence of foreign fighters in Mehurici. Now, my question is - and I don't know at all whether you could answer it - do you know anything about whether these are two different groups or one and the same group? If you read your two reports, the one on the 30th of July and the other on the 31st of July. When listening to you you put yourself the question, Are these the same people or not? Could you answer -- say anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally I did ask myself that question. Perhaps I would have visited the first group, as I had done in the 306th, the first group of 30 Arabs. But as I said I think in my statement -- in my report, the visit was approaching its end, we had returned to the battalion command, and then all of a sudden the superior command had asked that the issue of the Arabs be resolved. Upon arriving in the 306th when I encountered a similar problem and they weren't calling them Arabs then, they were calling them the Muslim forces, El Jihad, et cetera, well, yes the idea did occur to me that they weren't the same people. I didn't see those people over there, I don't know what they looked like. But the other group of people, yes, I did see them. And I did come to the conclusion that the same people were in question. Perhaps they were, but I didn't make such a claim. I didn't see this other group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I understand your answer. For the benefit of the Judges, could you tell where Bijelo Bucje is, in what part of Central Bosnia is it?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the Travnik sector. You pass through Turbe, then you turn towards a bend -- or rather, before the bend. It's to the left of Turbe. It's a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So it's west of Travnik I understand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Can you indicate how many kilometres?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could only guess. It's not far, it's not very far from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My other question has to do with your second report on the 306th Brigade. The issue has already been discussed. You wrote there in your report something, and I paraphrase from my memory, the brigade in Mehurici -- something should be done with the brigade in Mehurici. There are two possibilities and one of them is to declare them paramilitaries. And some questions have been put to you on that aspect of the problem, declaring people paramilitaries. What I want to know is: What are the consequences of declaring some groups of people paramilitary? For instance, if someone declared me to be a paramilitary, what would be the consequences for me? What risk would I incur or what other measures would I have to face? Could you tell me anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I'm a reserve officer. I didn't complete military academy. There are quite a few professional military issues that I didn't understand that well. So I really don't know what might have happened after having declared some unit to be a paramilitary unit. But if there is any other way in which I can be of assistance to you, I would be glad to help. What would have happened? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you are the person who proposes the -- this measure?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was my reasoning: I thought if someone proposed such a measure then it would no longer be possible for such a unit to remain in the area. It would have had to leave the area. It would no longer have presented a problem. As for the consequences or other consequences that might ensue, I didn't think about this. The commander who was in command of that unit, well I wanted him to have a clear situation. That's what I had in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the Judges' questions or following the Judges' questions, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution, if they have any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to Defence. They were speaking when I said that the Defence could ask additional questions in the framework of a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I only have one question that has to do with the questions put to the witness by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The report that I sent -- my first question is: Is a security organ in a military unit an organ which should have information on crimes committed? Does the commander rely on the security organ for such matters or on some other organ?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the security organ. There's no other organ. I can go through all the organs. That's the only organ that can deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you received this report, did you as the commander have any doubts about the information you had been provided with by the organ of security?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any information about this being an issue raised at a higher level. I only received an order from the corps command requesting that I provide them with information about events that took place for a certain period of time. But this document didn't state that President Izetbegovic or the UN was making such a request for information. I only received an order from the 3rd Corps. And when I received the report, I believe the matter to be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm now asking you as a commander, whether someone is interested in 25 men who were killed, is this an important matter for you?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If your security organ provides you with an explanation or provides you with information on how these 25 men were killed, do you believe that the way in which they explained the causes of death is important?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to go back to something I was saying earlier on. When I arrived in the command, I would examine all my assistants. When I came -- when I assumed a new post, I would talk to all the men. I didn't know what they knew and what they didn't know. The army was in the process of formation and I wanted to speak to the men to see what sort of men I was working with. I believed that Delalic was an honest man, a man of the people, somebody who certainly wouldn't have deliberately lied to me. So when I was provided with information on such important facts, there was really no reason for me to have any doubts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question as a commander, did you seriously examine the questions that were put to you and did you believe that you should provide information that you obtained from the organ to the command? Did you take this to be a serious matter or did you believe this is something you should deal with by the way so to speak?

utterances.speaker: VEZIR JUSUFSPAHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that I spoke about the matter to my first associates. It wasn't something that was set aside. As soon as many lives were at stake, I believed that the matter was very important. But I must repeat, I believed that my security organ had to be familiar with the case. I believed that they had all the necessary information because they were present there and I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this concludes your testimony. You have answered all the questions put to you over a period of two days. We thank you for having contributed to establishing the truth. And on behalf of the Chamber I wish you a good trip home, and naturally we wish you all the best now that you have retired. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now turn to the Defence. We have some time left at our disposal. According to my calculations, we have another three witnesses who will be appearing this week. We'll have a short break. We're obliged to have a technical break. We will resume at about 6.20 or 6.25, and then we'll try to continue after 7.15, if it's possible for the interpreters to do 15 additional minutes. Could you provide us with a little more information on the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given the testimony of this previous witness I can say that I can conclude the examination of the next witness by today. But I believe that we will have to continue with the examination of the witness tomorrow, rather of the cross-examination of the witness tomorrow. I believe that we will be able to conclude our examination of another witness, and I hope that we will be able to start hearing the next witness on Friday. We also have a witness who will be appearing here, so the second witness for tomorrow might continue testifying on Friday. And the witness scheduled for Friday might commence his testimony and conclude his testimony on Friday. According to my schedule my examination-in-chief shouldn't take longer than an hour, and in some cases my examination-in-chief will be briefer. I believe this will allow us to finish with the witnesses scheduled for this week by the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have our short break now, and we will resume at about 6.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we bring in the witness, I believe we have to resolve the issue of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence proposes that documents numbers 1360, 1406 -- excuse me -- no, I'll start over. The documents under IV entitled "Mujahedin," 1360, under number 1; then the one under number 6, 1389; under number 8, 1518; and under number 9, 1519 be introduced into evidence as Defence exhibits. We also wish to tender document under number 5 which has no English translation, it's 1404, be marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These two documents will be DH1360 and DH1360/E; DH1389 and DH1389/E; DH1518 with DH1518/E; and finally DH1519 and DH1519/E. These documents have already been marked for identification. The last document which is being marked for identification because it lacks a translation is DH1404 marked ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. First I have to check whether you can hear the interpretation of what I'm saying in your own language. If you do, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called by the Defence as a witness in the presentation of the Defence case. Before you make the solemn declaration, I have to ascertain your identity. So please tell me your full name as well as your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Suad Menzil. I was born on the 22nd of October, 1965, in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am employed in the federation army as an officer in the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1992 or 1993, more than ten years ago, at that time were you employed and did you have any rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not until -- no. Up to 1990 I was a student. And after that, I did not have any permanent employment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would you now please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the counsel who will examine you, I have to give you some information. At the outset there is something I've forgotten to say. Is this the first time you are testifying before any court, whether international or national, in connection with the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the first time I'm testifying before a court about these events. Although in 1997 or 1998, I think, I was asked to make a statement about genocide in Kotor Varos, but I didn't know anything about the case I was asked about. And the persons who questioned me probably decided they didn't need me as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today -- at the end of today we will answer the questions put to you by the Defence during what we call the examination-in-chief, and then tomorrow afternoon it will be the turn of the Prosecutors, who will cross-examine you. When this stage of the proceedings is over, and it should be over quite soon as they told me, the Defence should have some questions in re-direct examination, and the Judges whether for the sake of clarification or for some other reason may ask you some questions. Please try to answer the questions clearly because we don't know anything about you, we have no written documents. What you tell us will be entered into the record which is before you on the monitor in English, true to say, but this record will contain what you say during your testimony. Maybe somebody will show you documents and you will answer questions on the basis of those documents. If you find the question complicated, ask the person putting the question to repeat it. You have just made a solemn declaration that you will speak the whole truth. There's no need to say that you will not make a false statement, but there is something else that's important. In international proceedings when a witness does not wish to answer a question because he or she feels the answer one day will be used against them, the Chamber may make the witness respond to the question but will guarantee immunity in that case. I am giving you this information. I don't see how it can apply to you, but I want to tell you this. This is how your testimony will proceed. In the best possible conditions, we have about 40 minutes left today. In order not to waste anymore time, I will give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Menzil. I will ask you when you hear my question to pause a little so that the question can be interpreted and so that everyone in the courtroom can follow what we are saying. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Yes. I have to wait a few seconds. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Menzil, you may have misunderstood the President and you said that you did not have a job, although the question was about 1992 and 1993. Tell me, what were you doing actually in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, I understood the question to refer to the period up to 1992, so I apologise if I gave an erroneous answer. From the 11th of June until the 18th of October, 1992, I was part of the Kotor Varos Territorial Defence where I was the leader of a sanitary and veterinarian squad. This was the time of the aggression against Kotor Varos. And on the 18th of October, when I left the TO, I joined the unit which was called the 1st Kotor Varos Battalion. And it was composed of people who before the war had been employed abroad in Slovenia, Germany, and other places, and who had heard that there was resistance against the aggressor. So they established a unit in order to come and help us. This was a unit of mixed ethnic origin, as had been the Territorial Defence unit which I had belonged, and it was composed of Muslims, Orthodox, and Catholics. However, this 1st Battalion in Travnik was composed only of Catholics and Muslims. In that unit I spent a period of time. I was wounded. There were some 20 or so other men who were wounded and they had their destination in the barracks in Travnik where they organised a field hospital for us who had been wounded waiting for the outcome. At that time in Travnik there was a certain amount of chaos. The units of the army had not yet been officially established and the situation was quite undefined. So I felt it normal to join a unit from Kotor Varos which had already been established, and this was the Siprage Battalion which was in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, please tell me very briefly, what was your education before the war because as far as I was able to understand you said you had been a student. What were you studying and did you complete your studies?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, first I completed primary school and then secondary medical school. After that I went to the faculty of medicine in Pristina, and I was -- I had completed my course of studies but had not yet taken my final exams.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in Kotor Varos you were in the medical corps of the TO. Does this mean that although you had not yet gained your doctor's diploma, due to the wartime conditions you acted as a doctor in practice?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: My first war wounds date from that period. I knew what I had learned at university, but my first contact with real wounds and looking after them, even complicated ones, because we lacked sufficient staff we had to do these things, deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the 1st Siprage Battalion on Mehurici, when was this and what brigade was it part of?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: I arrived on the 22nd of December, 1992. And on the 25th of December, the 1st Siprage Battalion was established as the first battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade that was being formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, please tell me were you assigned any duty in that battalion?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I joined people who were well-informed and whom I knew from before, because they were people from Kotor Varos, there was a proposal which the brigade command accepted, and I was appointed leader or commander or officer for the sanitary and veterinarian squad.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, please tell me what sort of medical team did you have at your disposal and did you take any measures to equip yourselves in order to carry out your wartime activities?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: As I've already say, the army was in its infancy. It was a fledgling army, and the unit I belonged to, the battalion, was in a way in the beginning up to manpower levels. But as for the sanitary corps, we did not have sufficient staff. I only had one medical technician who hadn't even passed his professional exam. He was a young man just out of school and we didn't have professional staff, especially as regards the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Mehuric did you find any of your colleagues who were doctors, and if you did can you tell us how you organised the medical corps and provided medical assistance under these conditions?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, I think I have to explain what my approach was because I saw what the situation was, I understood that my first task was to set up this unit and to attempt to, as far as possible, find medical staff to organise the unit. Of course when we arrived at Mehuric, I contacted my superior command and I asked for someone from my profession. And there I found Dr. Ribic, an eminent specialist and an experienced doctor. And from that day I cooperated with him for as long as I was at Mehuric for the simple reason that he, as an older and more experienced colleague, helped me a lot in certain situations. And according to our ethics we had to work together, regardless of where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that short period of time, did you manage to organise the medical corps and train part of the population to help you as doctors?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Yes. The unit was in the process of being formed, but I have to say that the superior command and our commanding officers were full of understanding. And they tried to meet all our requests and adopt our suggestions so that very soon we were able to organise courses for nurses. We made a survey, a questionnaire, to find out who had the aptitude and who had a good secondary education, if nothing else. And some people among the civilian population were very interested, especially women. And we had two or three courses, and these courses proved to be highly effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who did you rely on for logistical support? Who provided you with medicines and sanitary material?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Of course I had to respect the military hierarchy, and that's how I acted. I received all the logistical support from the superior command, that is the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade. Let me clarify. My monthly requirements were sent to the chief of the medical corps who then approved them. And then we sent these to the 3rd Corps to supply what we required.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, did you draw any distinction when providing medical assistance between the civilian population and the military, or did you draw any distinction according to ethnic criteria when people asked for medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Of course we didn't. We didn't even -- it never even crossed our minds, because apart from our medical ethics and the oath that as a professional I was bound by, I was also bound by an oath I took when I joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this states quite clearly that we are duty-bound to protect the sovereignty and the constitutional order and so on and so forth of all citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time in Mehurici there were people of various ethnic origins, there were Catholics, there were Orthodox, and others, and this also applies to the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Mehuric, Mr. Menzil, did you observe the presence of foreigners from Afro-Asian countries?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Yes, I did observe the presence of foreigners, whether they were Afro-Asian, I don't know, but I saw that they were foreign, that they were different. And by their physical appearance I assumed that they might be from those countries, and this proved to be correct. Yes, of course I observed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the time after your arrival, did you notice that these foreigners had a certain attitude toward the local population and was there any division among the population in relation to these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: When I arrived, they were upstairs. My unit had a floor in a school and they were in the same school upstairs. They stayed there very briefly, but they kept one of the offices in the school for a longer period of time. I was unable to observe any divisions in the first few days because I was pre-occupied with organising the medical corps as I've just described. But I heard that they had a leader among them who had authority over them, they called him Sheikh and they obeyed him. His authority was unchallenged. In a short period, about the 20 days that they were there, I did not notice that they caused any problems or incidents. However, later on certain sparks began to fly and certain disagreements with the local population, primarily because they tried to impose religious ceremonies and a religious culture that was unacceptable, both to me and to many other people there. So of course conditionally speaking when I say "normal people," normal people despised them, marginalised them as far as their insistence on faith went. However, in this period in parallel with this, they tried to win over the local population by giving various kinds of humanitarian aid, even money. And I noticed people who did not belong to them who came to them for training. I don't know for what motive. Later it turned out that it was for material gain primarily. And one could feel that the local population was divided into those who supported them and those who did not support them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to discuss some specific events. Tell me please, if you can remember, what were you doing on the 24th of April? Does day remind you of an event in Mehurici or its vicinity that you wish to testify about?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Of course, it reminds me of a tragedy that unfortunately happened there. At that time and still today I become very emotional when I think of it. On the 24th of April I received information because part of our battalion was between the villages of Krpeljici and Bandol on the front line, and late one evening we received information that there had been an incident in one of our dugouts and our members were wounded. In the morning at about 10.00, I asked for the commander's approval, which I received, that I should go and see what happened, precisely what sort of incident and what the consequences were, and what could be done about it. I mean, at my level, I mean as far as providing medical assistance went. At about 10.00, I set out toward Krpeljici, and as I was leaving Mehurici I was stopped by two Arabs. I was in my medical vehicle. They stopped me and indicated someone was lying down beside them. I went out of the vehicle and saw that the man was wounded; he was also an Arab. He was wounded. And according to their gestures, they were asking probably that I provide assistance. I immediately approached him, took a look, realised that it was a complex wound, that it required hospitalisation, and we put the wounded man we found there in our ambulance and took him back to our centre where I did a primary -- I dealt with the wound and I knew an Arab who spoke Serbo-Croatian and I asked that this man be brought so that he could translate this. Ramadan was found, he arrived, and I told him that this wounded man whose wounds I had dressed should urgently be taken to the hospital in Zenica. As there was a blockade and the regional road was blocked we had to take a circuitous road through the woods another route. I asked that they find a vehicle, that's what I suggested, that they find a vehicle. I saw that they did have all-terrain vehicles, and that they take the men there urgently. And that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you knew an Arab called Ramadan?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know this Arab and how did you know what his name was?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, a few days after I arrived in Mehurici when the station was being established, early in the morning a local young man brought him to see me in the outpatients' clinic, and he said that he had been bitten by a dog. He showed me the dog bite. I dressed his wound and we talked a little bit, and he told me that he had been a student in Nis, and that's why he spoke Serbo-Croatian very well, and that he was from Syria. He didn't tell me anything else and I didn't ask him much, but that's how I know Ramadan. And later on I noticed that he was an intermediary at various times when people wanted to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This wounded man that you provided assistance to, did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, whenever you provide assistance, you have to identify the person. Of course I asked Ramadan to give me his details, and he pulled out a document which in my view was very odd. I'm still surprised by it. And it said the person bearing this pass must be allowed to pass through the Republic of Croatia and through territories under the control of the HVO as a humanitarian worker from Egypt. And it was signed by the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Josip Moric. This is the document I saw when I asked for identification, and it was probably because they entered as humanitarian workers that they obtained these passes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Menzil, what happened next on that day?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: When I had finished dealing with this wounded man, I again set out toward Krpeljic, that's where our brigade medical station was, where wounded soldiers were brought. I went down there and I saw that these two members of our unit had been handling a hand grenade, which had exploded. One's fist had been blown off; the other was seriously wounded. So this was actually an accident. And they were taken to hospital. I stayed there until some 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon. And then I went back and I saw a group of people of the local population in front of the station in Mehurici. I found Dr. Ribic inside the outpatients' clinic, and on the table was an elderly woman who had been seriously wounded and who, when I asked the doctor who she was, he said, "Don't ask. It's a woman from Miletici. She's seriously wounded. She's been brought here. We have to help her, look after her, and see how we can send her off to Zenica." And then together we took care of this woman. The wound was a very serious one; it was in the stomach area. And the urinary tract had been damaged. We introduced a catheter in order to prevent a kidney failure. And after we had dealt with this woman's wounds, we asked the civilian and military police to establish contact with the checkpoint at Unakovic [phoen] that was held by the HVO. And we said that the woman had to be urgently transported to Zenica in order for them to save her life because that's how bad the wound was, and to receive the treatment. However, some 20 minutes later or half an hour later, the people who went on behalf of the civilian and military police did not receive permission from the HVO checkpoint. We even told them the first and last name of this woman in order to propitiate them in some way, to pacify them, but they wouldn't let her through. Then we put her in the battalion vehicle and took her as far as Krpeljici, as it was night, and we had to go by a circuitous route through the woods. They were unable to take her to Zenica then; however, they did manage to take her in the morning, and thank God the woman survived. And somebody told she's still alive, and I'm very glad to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this wounded person was transferred there, did you find out about anything else that had happened that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, I first spoke to Dr. Ribic, but he himself wasn't clear about what had happened. He and the people who had brought the wounded person to him said that she had been wounded it Miletici. Naturally I went towards the base, to the school, which is where I had accommodation. That's where I slept. In the yard I saw a group of people who were nervous, agitated, I noticed that from Mehurici, Muhamed Arnaltovic, I used to see him and asked him what was happening. He said, confusion, there was a massacre in Miletici, the Mujahedin have expelled the people, there are people who have been killed. And then he said, they've taken Alija Delalic and Miso away. He started naming common friends of ours. He said they had taken them away up to the camp where they were located. I entered the command and in the command there was a state -- panic, it was very panic. Ribo Sulejman, the commander, was there and Dervis Suljic. He was completely pale. I asked him why, he said they had taken away his father, his uncle, all his relatives. I saw that they were trying to find a solution, to see how they could help these people, to see how they could get the civilians back as well as the people who weren't from Miletici. We even made a direct proposal, five or six of us who would volunteer, should go directly to their camp and request that they release these people. We set off. But then Ramadan appeared and we got hold of him, so to speak, to help us. We tried to persuade him to act as an intermediary, to establish contact with their supreme commander or their Emir, that's what they called him. Initially Ramadan hesitated, he said it wasn't his affair, it wasn't his business. But then he accepted. When Ramadan had gone, maybe about half an hour later, their Emir appeared escorted by armed members of his. Then Commander Lubenovic spoke to him. Sometimes the exchange was quite fierce, but he managed to persuade them to release the people, first the Suljics were released, and then Delic and Miso and all the other civilians who had been arrested were released from that camp up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, what did you then do with your neighbours from Miletici?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: They were my neighbours at the time, but that's not important. When I -- well, to tell you the truth, when I saw those people I re-experienced what had happened to my family in Kotor Varos, and I witnessed this myself, they were maltreated, they were expelled, et cetera. So this really affected me as a man and someone who worked in the medical field. When Mr. Ribo asked me whether I would go up there and see if it was necessary to give someone some sedatives or talk to someone, well naturally I didn't think about it. I asked my commander's authorisation; this was granted. I went up there and I remained -- I stayed with those people until the morning. I think I tried to help them to an extent. I think I was partially successful in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Menzil, did you find out about what had happened in the village?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, in conversation with the people who were there, naturally I found out what had happened in the village. They had told me about it. They claimed that the Mujahedin had attacked them, that Arabs had attacked them, that they appeared suddenly, unexpectedly, that they didn't know why they had appeared. The people were very agitated, there were some very difficult scenes. Family members would try to tell other family members that somebody had been killed, so there were difficult conversations. I had found out what had happened. Naturally they didn't know how many people had been killed, whether people had been killed, but they assumed that those who weren't there among them had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Menzil, tell me about the events at the beginning of June in Mehurici. Were you in Mehurici at the beginning of June and do you know anything about what happened on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, look, throughout the wartime period I was in Mehurici, or rather my command was located there. As a result, I had to be in that area, too. After the events in Ahmici, there were the events in Miletici. And then there were various other incidents down by [indiscernible] Jadol [phoen] et cetera. The situation had become so tense that they started cutting off roads, checkpoints were being erected, one could not circulate freely, and then naturally other forms of provocations appeared as a reaction. And I'm claiming with full responsibility that these were provocations. I don't know how to explain what happened later. I don't know how to explain the events before the 8th of June, because throughout the month of May the Zenica Mehurici -- Travnik and Mehurici road was blocked by the HVO. They were holding certain checkpoints. I even had an ugly experience when returning, when I was first authorised to replenish medical equipment in Zenica. When returning they sent us back from the checkpoint in Srednje. They would not allow us to pass through; this is in mid-May. What is even more absurd is that I left Zenica with one of our officers who was a member of the joint command which was supposing to be functioning at the time. He tried to intervene. He tried to contact Filipovic and solve the problem in this way, but he didn't let us pass through. And there were more serious forms of provocations because the brigade had been broken up in a certain sense. We heard that communications -- officer from the brigade had been killed by a sniper, that some people from the brigade were making members of the command to eat grass, and there was shooting directed attendant buildings, at rooftops, et cetera, every evening. Naturally, I thought that these were acts of provocation. I don't know if this is what caused the overall conflict, but these were provocative acts. The flag of the state of Croatia was put somewhere above Mehurici, or rather on a plateau above Mehurici and Krpeljici. I don't know why this flag had been erected. There was no border crossing there, but the flag was flying up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me what happened in the beginning of June. What do you remember from that period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, from the battalion commander I received an oral order stating that medical corps reception centre should be prepared and organised, they should prepare stretchers, medical equipment in companies and platoons for possible combat. Given the vast area covered by the Mehurici clinic with Dr. Ribic, I suggested we create two reception centres so that we could be as effective as possible if fighting broke out. On the 8th of June at 4.15 in the morning, the first wounded were delivered to me, unfortunately, two men who had run into mines and their limbs had been blown off. The roads were still blocked, so it was impossible to take them to hospital using the normal roads. We had to use a mountain road from Mehurici, and it took us an hour and a half for each wounded man, instead of about 20 minutes. That's how long it would have taken if the regular roads had been opened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether Mehurici was shelled and as a doctor, as a member of the medical corps, did you suffer any consequences?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, Mehurici was shelled, and both the reception centres, the clinic, and our battalion's reception centre were hit by the shells. The civilian clinic, two or three nurses, I can't remember exactly, the nurses who were supposed to receive the wounded were hit by shell fragments. I had one wounded man who was waiting and I was treating another one. But when the shell fell, the wounded man who was waiting to be treated was thrown to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether those were the only wounded persons who were taken to you or were there any other consequences of the combat over that period?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Well, as far as the wounded are concerned, apart from the wounded men from my unit, there were two HVO members who were wounded later. But before that in the afternoon hours, let's say when there was a lull in the fighting, Dr. Ribic came and said that some civilians had been taken to the barracks already, that there were quite a lot of women and children. He said that we should go and see what the situation was up there. Naturally we went up there and there were quite a few women and children who were there. We spoke to a doctor who was with them, (redacted).. I think her surname is (redacted)., but I'm not quite sure. I think her name was (redacted). She had a nurse with her. She knew Dr. Ribic because they had worked together in the hospital before, in a medical centre. I introduced myself and we said that they had all the medical equipment at their disposal, that we would place all the equipment we had at their disposal. All medical services would be placed at their disposal. And the warehouse where we had medical supplies was within the school. I gave her the key to the premises and said that she could use everything that we had available at that time. Naturally, we wanted to help, and if she thought there was anything we could do to help her, I said that we would be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your battalion offer those people any other form of assistance, the people who were taken there?

utterances.speaker: SUAD MENZIL
utterances.text: Yes. Well, a lot of people were suddenly taken to a very small area. I suggested that we take the necessary measures to prevent the spread of epidemics and to protect the building, the people who were there. I said that we should prepare toilets for use, and ensure that they could use them in a normal manner. After we had noticed that there were a lot of children there, I suggested to the commander that we should use our reserves, that we should use food that was appropriate for children and for the elderly so that civilian protection could help them in different ways as well. I said that we could provide them with milk in powdered form. Naturally this was done. And later civilian protection unit took charge of these duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you believe that we should adjourn now, I can do so. I have about another 15 questions, so if we cannot continue until half past 8.00 [as interpreted], I would be grateful if we could continue until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to bear the interpreters in mind, so we will have to adjourn. We'll resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. Doctor, you will have to return tomorrow. Try and return at about 2.00 p.m. You should be called into the courtroom at 2.15 and your testimony should be concluded sometime tomorrow afternoon. We will now adjourn and I invite everyone to appear for the hearing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
